## What This Is

A security fix. **If you installed v3.3.0, your Permanent Floor deletion gate has a hole in it, and you should apply this update.**

`pre-tool-approval-gate.sh` shipped in v3.3.0 as the gate that refuses unapproved deletion of your content files. It does not refuse. It refuses only when the deletion command happens to spell out your vault's full absolute path, which is the case that almost never occurs. An agent deleting a file the ordinary way, with a relative path, walks straight through the gate.

The gate was read, reviewed and shipped. It was never fired. That is the actual lesson here, and it is why this update ships a test rather than only a patch.

## The Defect

The gate asked the wrong question. It tested whether the vault root string appeared anywhere in the **command text**:

```sh
if in_vault "$COMMAND"; then    # wrong: inspects the command string
```

An agent working inside the vault deletes with a relative path, because that is what a working directory is for:

```sh
rm "Council Chamber/Codices/Humor Codex.md"
```

That command contains no absolute path, so the vault root string is absent, so `in_vault` returns false, so the gate allows it. The Floor consents. Meanwhile a harmless command that merely *mentions* the vault path would block, for the wrong reason.

Eight distinct paths through the gate were affected: `rm` with a relative path (quoted, bare and force-flagged), `powershell Remove-Item` and `cmd del` invoked from Bash, and `Remove-Item`, the `del` alias and `[System.IO.File]::Delete` on the PowerShell tool.

## The Fix

Classify on the **target path**, never on the command string.

```sh
if any_target_in_vault "$COMMAND"; then    # right: inspects each resolved target
```

Every protected-extension path token is pulled out of the command and classified individually:

- A **relative** path is bound to the working directory, and these hooks run with the vault as the working directory. Relative means internal. It blocks.
- An **absolute** path blocks only when it resolves inside the vault. This is what keeps scratch files, memory files and adapter paths outside the boundary freely deletable.

The polarity is now written into the file in prose, next to the code, because the inverted form reads as correct and is not.

## The Part That Matters More Than The Fix

**`Council Chamber/scripts/hooks/floor-gate-selftest.mjs` is new, and it is the point of this release.**

It is a positive control on the gate: twenty-one crafted inputs, sixteen that must be refused and five that must be allowed. The must-allow cases carry equal weight. A gate that blocks everything has traded a hole for a wall, and a wall is also a failure.

Run it after any edit to the gate, and on a cadence besides:

```sh
node "Council Chamber/scripts/hooks/floor-gate-selftest.mjs"
```

Exit 0 means the gate refused everything it must refuse and allowed everything it must allow. Exit 1 names each case that misbehaved.

Point it at the v3.3.0 gate and it reports `pass=13 fail=8`. Point it at the fixed gate and it reports `pass=21 fail=0`. That is what makes it an instrument rather than a decoration: it has been watched failing, so a pass from it means something.

Payloads are built with `JSON.stringify` rather than hand-quoted shell strings. An escaping mistake inside a test string produces a false negative that is indistinguishable from a guard failure, and a shell-quoted version of this probe produced exactly that once. Do not rewrite it in shell.

## The Governing Law Behind This Release

**Before trusting any negative result, prove the channel it depends on was live.**

A guard that has never refused anything is not known to work. A green suite that ran no assertions is not evidence, it is a mood. Absence is not a guard: a ceiling that holds because a file is missing or a flag is unset is a coincidence with good manners, and it holds until the day someone adds the file.

Ask of every ceiling in your ecosystem: does this **refuse**, or does it merely **not-happen**?

The formal discipline is mutation testing. Break the code on purpose, watch the test go red, restore it, watch it go green. Coverage says a line ran. A mutation score says a line mattered. Do it by hand when no tool is available, and never skip it because the suite was green last week. Green last week is the exact condition under which a guard rots unobserved.

## How to Implement

1. Replace `Council Chamber/scripts/hooks/pre-tool-approval-gate.sh` with the version in this release.
2. Add `Council Chamber/scripts/hooks/floor-gate-selftest.mjs` from this release.
3. Run `node "Council Chamber/scripts/hooks/floor-gate-selftest.mjs"` from your vault root. Confirm `pass=21 fail=0`.
4. If your vault root is not the working directory when hooks run, set `SOVEREIGN_VAULT_ROOT` to its absolute path. The self-test resolves the root the same way the gate does, so the two always agree on where the boundary is.

If step 3 does not go green, your gate is not protecting you, and the failing lines say exactly which door is open.

## If You Customized The Gate

Your copy is yours. Do not take this diff. Take the test.

Drop `floor-gate-selftest.mjs` into your vault, run it against your gate and read the failures. The spec is the twenty-one cases. How your gate satisfies them is your business. That is what a sovereign update looks like: the intent and the proof travel, and the code stays yours.

## Widening The Coverage

The gate protects one extension by default. Add more:

```sh
PROTECTED_EXTENSIONS="md txt canvas"
```

Then rerun the self-test. It reads the same variable, so widening the gate widens the proof.
